topics.title: Why Etiquette Exists
topics.short: Etiquette rests on three ideas: consideration for others' feelings, respect for every person, and honesty; its customs exist to put people at ease.
topics.trouble: Learners see etiquette as a set of snobbish rules for showing off. Every good custom has a reason, usually to spare someone discomfort; a rule used to embarrass someone defeats its own purpose.

topics.title: Manners and Etiquette
topics.short: Manners are the spirit (kindness and consideration); etiquette is the specific code (which fork, how to address an envelope), and it changes with time and place.
topics.trouble: Learners treat every etiquette rule as timeless. Many 1922 rules have changed, but the manners behind them, like thanking people and putting guests at ease, have not.

topics.title: When Customs Differ
topics.short: Customs vary by region, country and family; as a guest, follow your host's way, and never mock or correct another family's customs.
topics.trouble: Learners call a different custom "wrong," such as eating with the fork in the left hand or taking shoes off at the door. Different is not rude; correcting others is.

topics.title: Reading a Place Setting
topics.short: Bread plate on the left, drinks on the right; forks to the left of the plate, knives and spoons to the right, used from the outside in.
topics.trouble: Learners drink from the neighbor's glass or butter bread on the wrong plate. Make a lowercase b with the left hand and a d with the right: bread left, drinks right.

topics.title: The Formal Place Setting
topics.short: Each course has its own utensils, set in the order of use from the outside in, with dessert utensils above the plate and glasses above the knives.
topics.trouble: Learners panic at a long row of forks. Start with the outermost piece for each course, and when in doubt, watch the host.

topics.title: Using the Napkin
topics.short: Place the napkin on your lap after the host does, blot rather than wipe, leave it on your chair if you step away, and set it loosely left of the plate at the end.
topics.trouble: Learners tuck the napkin into a collar or leave it crumpled on the plate. Some writers say the chair, some the left of the plate, when stepping away; both are seen as polite.

topics.title: Bread and Glasses
topics.short: Tear off one bite-size piece of bread at a time and butter it over your bread plate; hold a stemmed glass by the stem and drink only from your own.
topics.trouble: Learners butter a whole roll at once or bite straight from it. One piece at a time is the custom.

topics.title: American and Continental Styles
topics.short: American style: cut, set the knife down, switch the fork to the right hand, eat tines up. Continental style: keep the fork in the left hand, tines down, and the knife in the right.
topics.trouble: Learners think one style is correct and the other rude. Both are correct in the U.S.; the key is to use one style smoothly, not to mix them clumsily.

topics.title: Resting and Finished Positions
topics.short: Resting: utensils on the plate, never on the table (in Continental style, crossed near the tips like an upside-down V, fork tines down). Finished: fork and knife side by side, diagonally, handles toward the lower right.
topics.trouble: Learners lean used utensils on the table or the rim like oars. Once used, a utensil stays on the plate; the finished position tells the server you are done.

topics.title: Courses and Service
topics.short: Wait until everyone is served or the host begins; at a large table, start when the host invites you. Food is traditionally served from the left and plates cleared from the right.
topics.trouble: Learners start as soon as their own plate arrives at a dinner party. At a large table the host may say "please start while it's hot," and then it is polite to begin.

topics.title: Tricky Foods
topics.short: Spoon soup away from you, twirl long pasta against the plate or a spoon, eat finger foods with fingers, and remove a pit or bone the way it went in.
topics.trouble: Learners spit a pit into the napkin or saw at food that should be eaten by hand. A pit or bone goes onto the fork or fingers and then to the plate's edge, quietly.

topics.title: Toasts
topics.short: The host usually gives the first toast; stand or raise your glass, keep it short and kind, and if the toast is to you, stay seated and don't drink to yourself.
topics.trouble: Learners think they must drink alcohol to join a toast. Raising any drink, even water, is fine; customs about toasting with water vary, but no one should press a guest to drink.

topics.title: Restaurant Manners
topics.short: Reserve if needed, arrive on time, be courteous to every server, order at a similar pace and price as your host, and raise problems quietly.
topics.trouble: Learners snap fingers or wave at servers, or send food back with a scene. A quiet "Excuse me, when you have a moment" works better.

topics.title: Who Pays and Splitting the Bill
topics.short: Traditionally whoever invites pays; with friends, agree before ordering whether to split evenly or pay for what you ordered.
topics.trouble: Learners split evenly after one person ordered far less, or argue at the table. Customs vary, so settle it early and cheerfully.

topics.title: Tipping in the U.S.
topics.short: At a sit-down restaurant in the U.S., about 15 to 20 percent of the bill before tax is customary, more for great service; tipping customs differ abroad.
topics.trouble: Learners tip on the total with tax and get confused, or carry U.S. tipping habits abroad where service is included or tipping is not expected. Percent amounts are a guide, not a law.

topics.title: Making Introductions
topics.short: Say the honored person's name first: an older person, a guest, a client, or a senior colleague; at work, rank decides, not age or gender.
topics.trouble: Learners avoid introducing people because they fear the order. Saying the names warmly matters far more than the order; a forgotten introduction is the real slip.

topics.title: Forms of Address
topics.short: Use titles such as Mr., Ms., Mrs., Mx. or Dr. with a last name until invited to use a first name, and use the name and title a person prefers.
topics.trouble: Learners use "Mrs." for any married-looking woman or guess at a title. "Ms." is safe for women; when in doubt, ask or listen for how a person introduces themselves.

topics.title: Handshakes and Other Greetings
topics.short: In the U.S., stand and shake hands firmly; elsewhere a bow, a nod or a cheek kiss may be usual, and some people prefer not to shake hands at all.
topics.trouble: Learners force a handshake on someone who has put a hand on their heart or bowed. Follow the other person's lead; a warm greeting can take many forms.

topics.title: Small Talk
topics.short: Small talk uses safe shared topics (the event, travel, books, food, the weather), open questions and real listening, and it leads to bigger conversations.
topics.trouble: Learners think small talk is shallow and skip it, or jump to personal questions about salary, age or plans for children. Light topics build trust first.

topics.title: Invitations
topics.short: A good invitation says who is hosting, what, when, where, what to wear if it matters, and how and by when to reply.
topics.trouble: Learners send invitations without an RSVP date or address, or let a guest guess whether a partner or children are invited. The envelope or message names exactly who is invited.

topics.title: Replying to an Invitation
topics.short: Reply by the date asked, in the way asked; "RSVP" asks for a reply either way, and "regrets only" asks only those not coming to reply.
topics.trouble: Learners reply "maybe," add guests who were not invited, or cancel at the last minute for a better offer. A reply is a promise.

topics.title: Arriving and Leaving
topics.short: Arrive on time for a dinner (not early), within a reasonable window for a party, and leave before the host looks tired; thank the host at the door.
topics.trouble: Learners arrive early "to help" and catch the host unready. For a meal, a few minutes after the stated time is fine; more than fifteen minutes late calls for a heads-up.

topics.title: Host Gifts
topics.short: A small host gift such as flowers in a vase, a treat or something for the pantry is welcome; it is for the host to enjoy later, not to serve that night.
topics.trouble: Learners expect the host to open and serve what they brought, or bring cut flowers that pull the host away to find a vase. Customs on host gifts vary by region.

topics.title: Hosting a Dinner
topics.short: Greet and introduce guests, ask about food needs ahead, seat the guest of honor at the host's right, keep the talk moving, and put guests at ease.
topics.trouble: Learners spend the party in the kitchen or apologize all night for the food. Guests remember a relaxed, welcoming host more than a perfect dish.

topics.title: Overnight Guests
topics.short: A good guest agrees on dates, follows the house routine, keeps their space tidy, offers to help, and sends a thank-you afterward; a good host gives towels, a key and a plan.
topics.trouble: Learners extend a stay without asking or expect to be entertained every hour. A clear arrival and departure date helps everyone.

topics.title: Thank-You Notes
topics.short: Write soon, name the gift or kindness, say how you will use or enjoy it, add a personal line, and close warmly; a handwritten note is still the warmest.
topics.trouble: Learners think an email or text never counts, or that a note sent late is worse than none. A late note is always better than no note.

topics.title: Condolence Notes
topics.short: Say you are sorry for the loss, share a memory or a good quality of the person, offer specific help if you can, and close with sympathy; keep it short.
topics.trouble: Learners say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing, or write "I know how you feel" or "everything happens for a reason." Simple, sincere words are best.

topics.title: Writing a Letter
topics.short: A letter has the date, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Grant,"), the body in short paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely," or "Warmly,") and your signature.
topics.trouble: Learners pick a closing that doesn't fit: "Love" for a business letter or "Yours truly" for a grandmother. Match the closing to how well you know the reader.

topics.title: Addressing an Envelope
topics.short: The recipient's name and address go in the center, your return address in the upper left, and the stamp in the upper right; use titles and full names.
topics.trouble: Learners write the return address in the center or the stamp on the left, or leave off the ZIP code. The post office reads the center block.

topics.title: Email Manners
topics.short: Write a clear subject, open with a greeting, keep it brief, proofread, reply within a day or two, and use "reply all" only when everyone needs it.
topics.trouble: Learners write emails in all capitals, skip the greeting, or reply-all to a whole list with "thanks!" Email is permanent and easy to forward.

topics.title: Phones in Company and in Public
topics.short: Silence the phone at meals, meetings and performances, step away for calls, and keep speakerphone and videos off in shared spaces.
topics.trouble: Learners think a phone face-down on the table is fine everywhere. Many hosts feel any phone on the table says "you might be interrupted"; at casual meals customs vary, at formal ones it stays away.

topics.title: Texting and Messaging
topics.short: Mind the hour, the tone and the length; don't send important or sad news by text when a call or visit is possible; answer within a reasonable time.
topics.trouble: Learners break up, resign or share a death by text. Serious news deserves a voice or a face.

topics.title: Social Media
topics.short: Ask before posting photos of others or their children, don't announce other people's news, and remember that posts are public and lasting.
topics.trouble: Learners post a group photo or a friend's engagement news before the people in it have shared it themselves.

topics.title: Video Calls and Meetings
topics.short: Join on time, check your sound and background, mute when not speaking, look at the camera, and give the meeting your attention.
topics.trouble: Learners multitask with the camera off and get caught when asked a question. Treat a video meeting like a room you walked into.

topics.title: Job Interviews
topics.short: Arrive a few minutes early, dress a step above the job's usual dress, greet everyone kindly, listen, ask good questions, and send a thank-you within a day.
topics.trouble: Learners are polite to the interviewer but curt with the receptionist. Everyone you meet may be asked what they thought of you.

topics.title: Dress Codes Decoded
topics.short: Social dress codes run from white tie and black tie to cocktail, smart casual and casual; at work, from business formal to business casual and casual. When unsure, ask the host.
topics.trouble: Learners read "black tie optional" as "jeans are fine" or "business casual" as athletic wear. Dressing for the occasion is a way of showing respect for the host.

topics.title: Meetings
topics.short: Be on time, come prepared, let others finish, keep to the topic, credit others' ideas, and follow up on what you promised.
topics.trouble: Learners interrupt to be seen as sharp, or repeat a colleague's idea as their own. Giving credit builds trust that lasts.

topics.title: The Office Kitchen and Shared Spaces
topics.short: Clean up after yourself, label and clear out your food, don't take what isn't yours, keep calls and smells modest, and refill what you empty.
topics.trouble: Learners leave a dish "to soak" for days or use the last of the coffee without making more. In shared spaces, leave it as you would want to find it.

topics.title: Wedding Guests
topics.short: Reply on time, bring only the guests named on the invitation, follow the dress code, give a gift (often from the registry), and let the couple shine.
topics.trouble: Learners bring a date who was not invited, or ask the couple why they were not given a plus-one. Whether guests should avoid all-white outfits is debated; most writers advise leaving white to the bride.

topics.title: Funerals and Memorials
topics.short: Dress in quiet colors, arrive early, sign the guest book, follow the family's customs, and offer the family short, sincere words: "I'm so sorry. She was a wonderful teacher."
topics.trouble: Learners stay away because they don't know what to say. Showing up matters most; customs for services differ by faith and family, so follow their lead.

topics.title: Visiting the Bereaved
topics.short: Keep visits short, listen more than you talk, offer specific help ("I'll bring dinner Tuesday"), and keep in touch in the weeks after.
topics.trouble: Learners say "Let me know if you need anything," which puts the work on the grieving person. A specific offer is easier to accept.

topics.title: Hospital Visits and New Babies
topics.short: Ask before visiting, keep it short, stay home if you are sick, wash your hands, and offer help with meals or errands rather than asking to hold the baby.
topics.trouble: Learners drop in unannounced or stay for hours. New parents and patients need rest more than company.

topics.title: Gifts and Regifting
topics.short: Choose with the person in mind, include a gift receipt when it may help, and thank every gift; regifting is debated, and most agree it must be new and never go back to the same circle.
topics.trouble: Learners regift a monogrammed or used item, or regift to a friend of the original giver. Opinions on regifting differ; care and discretion are what all sides agree on.

topics.title: Borrowing and Lending
topics.short: Ask, return the item on time in as good shape or better, replace what you break or use up, and lend only what you can afford to lose.
topics.trouble: Learners return a borrowed car with an empty tank or a dish unwashed. Returning it better than you found it is the custom.

topics.title: Being a Good Neighbor
topics.short: Greet neighbors, keep noise, pets and yard tidy, park considerately, warn them about a party or project, and talk to them directly about a problem.
topics.trouble: Learners complain to a landlord or online before a friendly word. A direct, friendly conversation solves most problems.

topics.title: Travel Courtesy
topics.short: On planes and trains, store bags quickly, recline gently, share the armrest (the middle seat gets both), keep calls short and quiet, and thank the crew and hotel staff.
topics.trouble: Learners slam the seat back or spread into a neighbor's space. Many travelers think the middle seat gets both armrests; it is a kindness, not a rule.

topics.title: Customs Abroad
topics.short: Before traveling, learn a greeting and "thank you" in the language, how people dress for sacred and formal sites, and the local customs on tipping, greetings and shoes.
topics.trouble: Learners assume American customs are universal: tipping, first names, loud talk or shorts in sacred places. Ask, watch and follow local ways.

topics.title: Forgetting a Name
topics.short: Admit it lightly ("I'm so sorry, your name has slipped my mind"), or introduce yourself first so they offer theirs; help others when they forget yours.
topics.trouble: Learners avoid the person or skip an introduction to hide the lapse. A brief, cheerful admission is better than an awkward evasion.

topics.title: Spills and Accidents
topics.short: Apologize briefly, help clean up, offer to pay for damage, and move on; as a host, reassure the guest and make light of it.
topics.trouble: Learners apologize over and over all evening, which keeps the attention on the accident. One sincere apology and a fix is enough.

topics.title: When Someone Else Slips
topics.short: Tell someone privately about spinach in their teeth or an open zipper; never correct another person's table manners or grammar in front of others.
topics.trouble: Learners point out another guest's etiquette mistake to show they know better. Correcting others publicly is the worse breach.

topics.title: Answering a Rude Remark
topics.short: Stay calm; ask "Why do you ask?", give a short neutral answer, change the subject, or simply say "I'd rather not discuss that."
topics.trouble: Learners answer rudeness with rudeness or feel they must answer a nosy question. You never owe a personal answer; a calm deflection keeps your dignity.

topics.title: Declining and Saying No
topics.short: Decline invitations, food and requests kindly and briefly ("Thank you for asking; I can't make it"); a long excuse isn't needed, and a lie isn't either.
topics.trouble: Learners invent elaborate excuses that get caught, or say yes and then don't show. A kind, clear no is both polite and honest.

topics.title: Asking and Answering
topics.short: Ask clearly and in person or by call, make plans specific, and accept a "no" gracefully; answer kindly and truthfully either way.
topics.trouble: Learners keep asking after a no, or say "maybe" to avoid saying no. A clear, kind answer respects both people.

topics.title: Courtesy on a Date
topics.short: Be on time, put the phone away, listen, be kind to staff, and settle who pays ahead; customs range from the inviter paying to splitting, and both are polite.
topics.trouble: Learners assume there is one rule about who pays. Writers disagree; what matters is that it is settled without pressure or awkwardness.

topics.title: Posture and Presence
topics.short: Stand tall and relaxed, sit upright, rise to greet, look people in the face, and keep hands still; presence means giving people your full attention.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse poise with stiffness or think presence is about looking important. Calm attention to others is what people remember.
